title: Redwood cost econ discovery with Hemisphere Capital

Key threads: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, batching and KV/prefix caching benefits, expected throughput (200 qps peak), budget guardrails, and pilot next steps including benchmark run and pricing sheet.

header:
Date: 2026-03-17
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marc Delaney (Hemisphere CTO), Sofia Ruiz (Head of ML), Ethan Park (Infra), Lena Ortiz (Product)
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then we'll jump into economics and the questions you sent.
[00:08] Marc: Hey yeah Marc here, thanks. We're excited — just to be clear our primary constraint is cost per inference and hitting budget for production.
[00:15] Avery: Got it, cost/unit is the focus. Priya and I will walk through levers: per-token rates, batching, prefix/K-V cache, and then host vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs.
[00:28] Priya: quick note, I'll call it KV cache sometimes or K-V cash in notes, transcription sometimes spells it weird.
[00:34] Sofia: haha noted. On our side — we expect about 12M tokens a month initially, spiking to ~50M in 3 months if the pilot goes well. Peak qps around 150-200. Latency SLO ideally under 500ms tail.
[00:49] Avery: ok that helps. For hosted, our per-token published rates for our curated open models are X cents/token for prompt and Y cents/token for completion (note: in call we'll discuss ranges). For dedicated, you move to a reserved GPU pool with lower unit cost but commit monthly. Private has higher fixed platform fee but gives you full control and avoids egress.
[01:12] Marc: can you quantify "lower unit cost"? like is dedicated 2x cheaper or 10x cheaper?
[01:18] Priya: depends heavily on utilization and batching. Example: if you get 60-80% GPU utilization with good batching, per-token cost decreases a lot — we often see 30-60% reduction vs hosted list rates after reserved capacity amortization. But if utilization is low, dedicated can be more expensive.
[01:36] Ethan: What's batching sensitivity? our requests are short, avg 40 tokens completion, 60 tokens total.
[01:43] Priya: short responses make batching harder. However, continuous batching and micro-batching inside the runtime still helps. Also prefix/K-V caching is big for applications with repeated prompts or system messages — you can avoid re-encoding the entire prompt. In practice caching can cut token compute by 20-50% depending on reuse.
[02:05] Lena: our product uses a lot of templated prompts so cache hit rates should be decent.
[02:10] Marc: how does this translate to $/1M tokens?
[02:14] Avery: rough hosted example: for our base open curation model, hosted might be around $15-$25 per million tokens end-to-end depending on prompt/completion split and streaming overhead. Dedicated typical effective cost could be $6-$12 per million at good utilization. Private is similar to dedicated after platform fee, but includes infra ops and KMS integration. (note: numbers are illustrative on call)
[02:37] Sofia: those ranges help. We have a hard budget target of $8 / 1M tokens long-term.
[02:42] Priya: to hit $8, you'd likely need dedicated with high utilization and aggressive batching/quantization, or private if you can amortize infra. Also model variant matters — smaller quantized models cost much less per-token but may have quality tradeoffs.
[02:58] Marc: what about quantization? can you support int8/int4 on dedicated/private?
[03:03] Priya: yes we support multiple quantization profiles. There's a quality vs cost tradeoff; int8 often gives similar quality with ~1.5-2x perf improvement and cost reduction compared to fp16. int4 is more aggressive but can still be viable for some tasks. We run evals on your prompt sets to recommend the minimal quant that meets your quality bar.
[03:23] Ethan: latency impact? quantization helps latency generally.
[03:26] Priya: yes lower-precision kernels reduce memory and improve kernel throughput; so tail latency and throughput both improve, which helps unit cost.
[03:33] Marc: security/regulatory — we may need SOC 2 and KMS. Is that available on hosted?
[03:38] Avery: hosted has SOC 2 and enterprise contract options; but for customer-managed KMS and full network isolation you'd be looking at Dedicated with VPC peering or Private deployment. Private gives you the most control for compliance.
[03:52] Sofia: for dedicated, does Redwood manage ops or do we need to operate?
[03:56] Priya: Redwood operates the serving runtime; for Dedicated we manage the GPU pools in our infra but network is isolated. For Private we ship a control plane you can host or we can deploy into your VPC depending on contract.
[04:08] Marc: ok back to economics — can you walk through a sample calc for our 12M tokens/month?
[04:13] Avery: sure quick calc: hosted at $20 / 1M -> 12M = $240; dedicated optimized at $8 / 1M -> 12M = $96; plus overheads (for dedicated you have commit/seat fees, for private add a platform license maybe a few thousand monthly). Also consider caching — if cache reduces compute by 30%, effective tokens billed/compute becomes 8.4M, so cost drops proportionally.
[04:42] Sofia: what's the billing unit exactly — do you charge based on tokens generated only or both prompt+completion?
[04:47] Avery: we bill for both prompt and completion tokens. We also report token breakdown in the Console so you can see cost per-route.
[04:54] Marc: and for streaming? any extra overhead?
[04:57] Priya: streaming can increase small per-request overhead due to connection time but per-token compute cost is similar; doing many tiny responses is the expensive pattern — batching mitigates that.
[05:08] Lena: sample pilot idea: we want to run a 2-week pilot covering 1M tokens/day for a small cohort of customers to validate latency and cost.
[05:18] Avery: that works. For pilot we can run hosted initially for quick turn, then move to short-lived dedicated pool for a canary to measure unit economics. Priya will help with benchmark script.
[05:29] Marc: is there a way to cap spend automatically? we can't exceed budget.
[05:33] Avery: yes Redwood Console supports per-route quotas and alerts, and we can set hard caps that will reject requests beyond the budget. For Dedicated you can also do autoscale policies that limit burst capacity.
[05:44] Ethan: networking question: if we do private, what's the egress pattern? we need to keep data in region.
[05:49] Priya: Private lets you keep traffic in your VPC; no egress to public internet. Dedicated hosted can be regionally isolated but may still transit provider networks — we can address with contract language and peering.
[06:02] Marc: are there any hidden costs like tokenization differences or encoding overhead?
[06:06] Priya: tokenization differences matter if you move between model families. We surface tokenization counts in the console; effective tokens can change if you switch models. Also prompt engineering to reduce token count is an oft-ignored lever.
[06:19] Sofia: can you demo the Console cost breakdown in the pilot?
[06:22] Avery: yes we'll include a short Console walkthrough in the pilot kickoff.
[06:26] Marc: competitor question — we've looked at OpenAI and Anthropic; how does Redwood compare?
[06:31] Avery: Redwood focuses on serving flexibility and unit economics — same interface across hosted/dedicated/private, and tooling to tune batching/caching/quantization to reduce $/token. With OpenAI/Anthropic you get managed models but less control over dedicated/private deployments and less transparency into unit economics. Self-hosted Triton gives control but requires you to build orchestration and ops.
[06:53] Priya: another note: model routing and fallbacks can reduce cost spikes — e.g., route to cheaper quantized variant on load. That requires evals to ensure quality alignment.
[07:06] Marc: ok what's needed from us to run the benchmark?
[07:10] Priya: sample prompts (3-5), expected distribution of sequence lengths, target throughput, and sample dataset for eval. We'll provide a runbook to reproduce.
[07:20] Sofia: we can share prompts and token estimates by Friday.
[07:24] Avery: perfect. We'll follow up with pricing sheet and scheduling. Any other questions on economics?
[07:29] Marc: one last: how do you handle token-level caching auditing — we need audit logs if we're caching customer prompts.
[07:36] Priya: we keep audit logs and can configure whether cached keys are stored in plaintext; for sensitive cases we can use ephemeral caches or ensure cache keys are hashed and KMS-managed. We'll include security doc.
[07:50] Lena: that covers it for us.
[07:53] Avery: recap: I'll send pricing and TCO, Priya the runbook, you send prompts and token estimates — pilot kickoff next week tentatively. Thanks everyone.
[08:04] Marc: thanks all.
[08:06] [call ends]
notes: Transcription includes occasional mis-hearings (e.g., 'K-V cash' for KV cache). Customer very focused on hitting $8 per 1M tokens target; pilot agreed to validate levers. Security and KMS are gating items for private deployment.
